cues.text: Chapter six is a model essay, and it answers a classic exam-style question: design a scalable and resilient enterprise network.
Let's walk through how a strong answer is built, one move at a time.
The first thing a defensible answer does is begin by identifying users, workload, locations and critical services.
Before you draw a single switch, you must know who will use the network, what traffic they will generate, where they are physically located, and which services the organisation cannot afford to lose.
Every later design choice is justified by these four things.
Next, the essay uses a hierarchical architecture with three layers: access, distribution and core.
It combines this with a hybrid topology, meaning a mixture of topology types rather than one pure shape.
The source gives three reasons for this design, and each one matters.
First, access switches simplify fault isolation.
Because end devices connect to access switches, a problem at one edge can be located and contained there, without confusing the whole network.
Second, redundant routed backbone paths protect critical connectivity.
If one path through the backbone fails, a second routed path can carry the traffic, so critical services stay reachable.
Third, modular access blocks support growth.
When the organisation expands, you add another access block built the same way, instead of redesigning everything.
The essay then says to segment business functions into VLANs and subnets, and to enforce explicit policy between them.
A VLAN is a virtual local area network, a logical separation of devices at layer two, and a subnet is the matching separation at the IP layer.
So, for example, finance, staff, guests and servers can each sit in their own segment.
The key word is explicit: traffic between segments should only be allowed where a clear rule says so, rather than flowing freely.
Now, on media and bandwidth, the source tells us to choose them from measured traffic and growth, not theoretical maximums alone.
In other words, don't simply pick a link because its rated top speed looks impressive.
Measure what the network really carries, add expected growth, and size the cabling and capacity from that evidence.
Theoretical maximums are still part of the picture, but they must not be the only basis.
Security and operations come next.
Protect management with authenticated access, firewalls and monitoring.
That means only verified administrators can reach the management functions of devices, firewalls control what can reach them, and monitoring lets you notice problems or misuse.
Alongside this, provide backup power and tested failover.
Notice the word tested: a failover mechanism that has never been tried is only a hope, not a design guarantee.
The essay also requires documentation.
Document addressing, routing, equipment, policy and test criteria.
That covers the IP addressing plan, the routing design, the list of equipment, the security and segmentation policy, and the criteria you will use to test that the network works as intended.
Then comes the comparison, which is what makes an answer persuasive.
Compare cheaper single-star and expensive full-mesh alternatives.
A single star, with everything connected to one central point, is cheaper but leaves that centre as a single point of failure.
A full mesh, where every node connects to every other, offers great redundancy but is expensive.
Your hierarchical hybrid design sits between these two extremes.
Finally, the conclusion.
The essay concludes that scalability, resilience, security, cost and operational simplicity must be balanced.
No single goal wins outright.
A good network architect weighs all five, and a good exam answer says so explicitly at the end.
